title: Anaesthesia, Emergency Medicine and Critical Care
description: Preoperative assessment, general and regional anaesthesia, airway management, resuscitation, trauma and shock, and intensive care.

topics.title: Preoperative Assessment and General Anaesthesia
topics.summary: ASA classification, fasting, airway assessment, anaesthetic agents and monitoring.

notes.b: Preoperative assessment identifies risks and optimises patients: history (previous anaesthetics and complications, family history of malignant hyperthermia or suxamethonium apnoea, comorbidities, drugs, allergies), examination, and investigations as indicated (e.g. FBC, electrolytes, sickle cell screening — genotype — is important in Nigeria, ECG in older patients). The ASA physical status classification: I (healthy), II (mild systemic disease), III (severe systemic disease), IV (severe disease that is a constant threat to life), V (moribund, not expected to survive without surgery), VI (brain-dead organ donor); 'E' denotes emergency. Fasting: 6 hours for solid food, 4 hours for breast milk, 2 hours for clear fluids. Airway assessment: Mallampati class (I–IV), mouth opening, thyromental distance, neck movement. Anticoagulants, antiplatelets and some antidiabetics may need adjustment.
k: Fasting: 6 h solids, 2 h clear fluids

notes.b: General anaesthesia comprises hypnosis, analgesia and (when needed) muscle relaxation — the triad. Induction: IV agents — propofol (smooth, antiemetic, causes hypotension), thiopentone, ketamine (dissociative; maintains blood pressure and airway reflexes; bronchodilator; widely used in Nigeria and for field anaesthesia; emergence reactions), etomidate (cardiovascular stability). Inhalational agents: sevoflurane (pleasant — used for gas induction in children), isoflurane, halothane (still used in resource-limited settings; hepatitis, arrhythmias), nitrous oxide. MAC (minimum alveolar concentration) measures potency. Muscle relaxants: suxamethonium (depolarising — rapid onset for rapid sequence induction; causes hyperkalaemia, malignant hyperthermia trigger) and non-depolarising (rocuronium, atracurium, vecuronium — reversed by neostigmine with glycopyrrolate or by sugammadex for rocuronium). Standard monitoring: ECG, non-invasive BP, pulse oximetry, capnography (ETCO2 — confirms tracheal intubation), temperature and anaesthetic agent concentration. Malignant hyperthermia is treated with dantrolene.
k: Ketamine: preserves BP and airway reflexes

topics.title: Regional and Local Anaesthesia
topics.summary: Local anaesthetic pharmacology, spinal and epidural anaesthesia, nerve blocks and toxicity.

notes.b: Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated sodium channels, stopping nerve conduction. Amides (lidocaine/lignocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine — metabolised in the liver) and esters (procaine, tetracaine — metabolised by plasma esterases, more allergenic). Maximum doses: lidocaine 3 mg/kg (7 mg/kg with adrenaline), bupivacaine 2 mg/kg. Adrenaline (vasoconstrictor) prolongs action and reduces toxicity but traditionally avoided in end-arteries (digits, penis) — modern evidence suggests dilute adrenaline in digits is safe. Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST): circumoral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, agitation, seizures, then cardiovascular collapse (bupivacaine is especially cardiotoxic). Treatment: stop injection, airway, treat seizures with benzodiazepines, CPR if needed, and intravenous lipid emulsion (20% Intralipid).

Spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthesia injects local anaesthetic (usually hyperbaric bupivacaine) into the CSF below L1/L2 (usually L3/4 or L4/5 — Tuffier's line joining the iliac crests is at L4) — rapid, dense block; the commonest anaesthetic for caesarean section in Nigeria. Epidural anaesthesia uses a catheter in the epidural space — slower, titratable, used for labour analgesia and postoperative pain. Complications: hypotension (sympathetic block — treat with fluids and vasopressors such as ephedrine or phenylephrine; left uterine displacement in pregnancy), high/total spinal, post-dural puncture headache (postural, worse on sitting; treat with fluids, analgesia, caffeine, epidural blood patch), urinary retention, and rarely epidural haematoma or abscess. Contraindications: patient refusal, coagulopathy or anticoagulation, infection at site, raised ICP, severe hypovolaemia. Peripheral nerve blocks (ultrasound-guided) — brachial plexus, femoral, TAP blocks — provide targeted analgesia.

topics.title: Airway Management and Resuscitation
topics.summary: Airway manoeuvres, intubation, BLS and ALS algorithms and post-resuscitation care.

notes.b: Basic airway manoeuvres: head tilt–chin lift, jaw thrust (in suspected cervical spine injury), suction, oropharyngeal (Guedel — sized from the incisors to the angle of the jaw) and nasopharyngeal airways (avoid in basal skull fracture), and bag–valve–mask ventilation. Supraglottic airway devices (laryngeal mask airway, i-gel) are rescue and routine devices. Tracheal intubation with direct or video laryngoscopy secures the airway; Cormack–Lehane grades describe the laryngoscopic view. Difficult airway guidelines (e.g. DAS) emphasise oxygenation: if 'can't intubate, can't oxygenate' (CICO), perform front-of-neck access (scalpel cricothyroidotomy). Rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure (debated) is used for patients at risk of aspiration (full stomach, pregnancy, bowel obstruction).
k: Avoid NPA in basal skull fracture

notes.b: Adult basic life support: check safety, response and breathing (no normal breathing — call for help and an AED), start CPR at 30:2 with chest compressions at 100–120 per minute and depth 5–6 cm, allowing full recoil and minimising interruptions. Advanced life support: shockable rhythms (ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia) — defibrillate, resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes; adrenaline 1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes after the third shock; amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock. Non-shockable rhythms (asystole, pulseless electrical activity) — adrenaline 1 mg as soon as possible, CPR. Treat reversible causes — the 4 Hs (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia and metabolic, hypothermia) and 4 Ts (thrombosis — coronary or pulmonary, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins). Post-resuscitation care: oxygenation (SpO2 94–98%), blood pressure, glucose, temperature control and treating the cause. Paediatric BLS starts with 5 rescue breaths, then 15:2.

topics.title: Trauma and Shock
topics.summary: Primary survey (ATLS), haemorrhage control, types of shock and fluid resuscitation.

notes.b: Trauma is a major cause of death among young Nigerians (road traffic crashes — especially motorcycles and tricycles, falls, gunshots and violence). The ATLS primary survey follows <C>ABCDE: catastrophic haemorrhage control (direct pressure, tourniquet), Airway with cervical spine protection, Breathing (look for tension pneumothorax — treat with needle decompression then chest drain; open pneumothorax — three-sided dressing; massive haemothorax; flail chest), Circulation with haemorrhage control (two large-bore cannulas, bloods including cross-match; identify bleeding in chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones and externally — 'blood on the floor and four more'; pelvic binder), Disability (GCS, pupils, glucose), and Exposure/Environment (prevent hypothermia). Adjuncts: FAST ultrasound, chest and pelvic X-rays. The secondary survey is a head-to-toe examination with an AMPLE history (Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last meal, Events).
k: Blood on the floor and four more

notes.b: Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion. Types: hypovolaemic (haemorrhage, dehydration — the most common in trauma), cardiogenic (pump failure), obstructive (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, massive PE), and distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic — spinal cord injury causes hypotension with bradycardia). Haemorrhagic shock classes (ATLS): class I (< 15% blood loss — minimal changes), class II (15–30% — tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure), class III (30–40% — hypotension, confusion), class IV (> 40% — life-threatening). Management: control bleeding, permissive hypotension (target systolic about 80–90 mmHg until bleeding controlled, except head injury), balanced resuscitation with blood products (massive transfusion protocols 1:1:1), limited crystalloid, tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury, and early surgery ('damage control'). Septic shock: early antibiotics, fluids and vasopressors (noradrenaline). Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg.

topics.title: Intensive Care and Perioperative Medicine
topics.summary: ICU admission, ventilation basics, sepsis management, fluids, pain and postoperative complications.

notes.b: Intensive care supports failing organs: mechanical ventilation (invasive or non-invasive — CPAP, BiPAP), vasopressors and inotropes, renal replacement therapy, and sedation. Nigeria has few ICU beds, concentrated in tertiary hospitals; triage and early recognition of deterioration (early warning scores such as NEWS2) improve outcomes on wards. Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection (Sepsis-3); qSOFA (respiratory rate ≥ 22, altered mentation, systolic BP ≤ 100) flags risk. The sepsis bundle: measure lactate, take blood cultures before antibiotics, give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4, and vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥ 65 mmHg. ARDS (acute respiratory distress syndrome) is managed with lung-protective ventilation (tidal volume 6 mL/kg ideal body weight, plateau pressure < 30 cmH2O) and prone positioning.

Maintenance fluid requirements: about 25–30 mL/kg/day water with sodium, potassium and glucose (Holliday–Segar 4-2-1 rule in children: 4 mL/kg/h for the first 10 kg, 2 for the next 10, 1 thereafter). Postoperative complications: primary haemorrhage, pain, nausea and vomiting (PONV — risk factors: female, non-smoker, history of PONV, opioids), atelectasis (day 1–2 fever), pneumonia, urinary retention, wound infection (day 5–7), anastomotic leak, DVT/PE (prophylaxis with early mobilisation, compression and low-molecular-weight heparin), and paralytic ileus. Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocols (limited fasting, carbohydrate loading, multimodal analgesia, early feeding and mobilisation) shorten hospital stays. Multimodal analgesia combines paracetamol, NSAIDs, regional techniques and opioids as needed.
